claims.text: Multi-element grain-boundary segregation governs the structural stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature by kinetically inhibiting grain-boundary migration.
Multi-element grain-boundary segregation governs chemical stability by inhibiting phase transformations.
The initial alloy is nanocrystalline and has a homogeneous, random distribution of multiple constituent elements.
A post-synthesis thermal treatment can promote multi-element segregation at grain boundaries.
Multi-element segregation modifies grain-boundary chemical composition and structure.
Decoration by multiple alloying elements raises the activation energy for grain-boundary migration.
Decoration by multiple alloying elements raises the activation energy for grain-boundary sliding.
Multi-element grain-boundary segregation inhibits grain-boundary migration and sliding.
Inhibition of grain-boundary migration retards high-temperature coarsening.
Grain-boundary decoration suppresses phase transformations at elevated temperatures.
Grain-boundary kinetic stabilization is more influential than sluggish diffusion in the bulk lattice.
Samples with pronounced grain-boundary segregation will exhibit slower grain growth than untreated samples.
Samples with pronounced grain-boundary segregation will show a delayed onset of phase separation.
Samples with pronounced grain-boundary segregation will show a delayed onset of amorphization.
Samples with pronounced grain-boundary segregation will retain mechanical strength better at high temperature than untreated samples.
The proposed mechanism should dominate when nanoscale grain boundaries are the main sites of structural degradation.
The effect should be less pronounced in coarse-grained alloys.
The effect should be less pronounced when bulk-diffusion effects override grain-boundary effects.
